title: Market Research
text:
Global markets are exhibiting a fragile equilibrium as elevated bond yields and geopolitical oil shocks test the prevailing equity thesis without entirely breaking it [ubs.com]. Over the past three months, the MSCI World Index has hovered near all-time highs, supported by resilient corporate earnings, even as the 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.73% and Brent crude pushed toward $94 per barrel amid Middle East tensions [stifel.com]. While headline inflation has moderated to 3.0% in the US, core stickiness and rising energy costs suggest the return to 2% stability remains elusive, leaving central banks in a cautious holding pattern [fortemfin.com]. Consequently, global growth equities are experiencing a tug-of-war between robust AI-driven earnings momentum and the creeping realization that the macroeconomic backdrop is far less benign than the market’s low-volatility complacency implies [lseg.com].



MSCI World Equity Index


Transitioning to the domestic landscape, the S&P 500 closed at 7,674.37 and the Nasdaq 100 at 29,308.86 at the end of August 2026. These levels reflect a market that has successfully digested the 2022-2023 rate shock but is now grappling with a new paradigm where liquidity is no longer expanding, yet earnings growth remains surprisingly robust. Gold has surged to $4,661.60 in August 2026, reflecting deep-seated fiat debasement fears and geopolitical hedging [fieracapital.com]. We are seeing a distinct resemblance to the late stages of the 1999 dot-com melt-up and the 2006 pre-credit crunch cycle. During those periods, equity indices grinded higher on the back of technological optimism and narrow leadership, while underlying macroeconomic friction was largely ignored by a complacent volatility complex.



Performance of Major US Stock Indices


The S&P 500 trailing P/E ratio stood at 29.58 in August 2026, a valuation premium that echoes the expansive multiples of 1999 and the peak optimism of 2021. What makes this environment particularly treacherous for growth investors is the extreme complacency in the derivatives and credit markets. The VIX closed at 15.13 at the end of August 2026, and the ICE BofA High Yield Option-Adjusted Spread compressed to a tight 2.75%. Historically, when credit spreads are this tight and volatility is this subdued while oil prices are elevated, it indicates that the market is pricing in a flawless economic landing, completely discounting the drag that energy costs exert on consumer discretionary and corporate margins.



S&P 500 PE Ratio


The macroeconomic data paints a picture of a paralyzed Federal Reserve and a slowing real economy. The Fed Funds Target Rate has been anchored at 3.75% since late 2025, trapped between a CPI that remains stubbornly at 3.0% as of July 2026 and a Q2 2026 real GDP growth estimate of just 1.5%. This stagflationary undertone is heavily influenced by Brent crude, which reached $93.87 in August 2026. Furthermore, the yield curve has fully un-inverted, with the 2-year Treasury at 4.20% and the 10-year at 4.68% at the end of August 2026. While a positive 48-basis-point spread might seem benign, historical patterns from 2000 and 2006 demonstrate that the phase immediately following a prolonged inversion is often when the real economy finally cracks under the weight of cumulative monetary tightening.



US 2Y and 10Y Treasury Yields and Spread



Risks:

Energy-Driven Margin Compression: With Brent crude at $93.87 in August 2026 and CPI stuck at 3.0%, the input cost pressures reminiscent of the 2021-2022 inflationary scare threaten to stall the margin expansion that growth stocks rely on. If the Fed is forced to halt or reverse its easing cycle due to a secondary inflation spike, the duration-sensitive long end of the growth portfolio will suffer severe multiple compression.
Yield Curve Un-Inversion Recession Signal: The 10-year yield at 4.68% and 2-year at 4.20% represents a positive spread, but historically, the phase immediately following a prolonged inversion is when the real economy cracks. A sudden spike in the BofA HY spread from its current tight 2.75% would trigger a violent repricing of unprofitable tech and high-multiple compounders.

Opportunities:

AI Infrastructure & Energy Beneficiaries: Just as the late 1990s saw telecom infrastructure build-outs, today’s AI capex cycle requires massive physical infrastructure. Companies providing power generation, grid modernization, and cooling solutions are uniquely positioned to benefit from both the tech boom and the elevated energy pricing environment, acting as a bridge between growth and real assets.
Pricing Power in Mission-Critical Software: In an environment where CPI is sticky at 3.0% and household debt service payments are elevated at 11.16% of disposable income as of Q1 2026, enterprises will cut discretionary spending but maintain mission-critical software. Growth companies with high gross margins and essential enterprise workflows can pass through inflationary costs, acting as a hedge against the broader macro slowdown.


Given the robust secular tailwinds of the AI investment cycle but the increasingly hostile macroeconomic backdrop, I suggest a 50-75% portfolio exposure to US growth stocks. The earnings momentum is real, and the underlying fundamentals of the technology leaders remain intact, preventing a broad-based bear market. However, the era of the “Fed put” and zero-interest-rate liquidity is over. With oil near $94, sticky 3% inflation, and a paralyzed central bank, we must discard speculative, unprofitable duration in favor of cash-flow generative compounders. Maintaining a 25-50% buffer in short-duration credit, quality fixed income, or cash provides the necessary dry powder to deploy if the VIX spikes or credit spreads widen, ensuring we can capitalize on volatility rather than being victimized by it.

title: About
text:
This project combines historical and real-time financial data with AI to produce automated research reports for US growth stock investors. By feeding macroeconomic indicators, equity market data, and commodity prices into an AI model, each report identifies historical patterns, draws parallels to current conditions, and highlights risks and opportunities for growth-oriented portfolios.
All charts and visualizations in the reports are created by the author — the AI generates only the written analysis.

Data Sources
Every report is grounded in real data from:

FRED (Federal Reserve Economic Data): Inflation (CPI), GDP growth, unemployment, Fed balance sheet, Treasury yields, household debt, recession indicators, Fed funds rate, and high-yield credit spreads
Yahoo Finance: MSCI World Index, S&P 500, NASDAQ 100, Dow Jones, VIX, gold, and Brent crude oil
Multpl.com: S&P 500 trailing P/E ratios
